lessons.title: Polygon and parallel-line angles
lessons.summary: Explain polygon angle sums and use angle relationships to find missing values.
lessons.objective: Explain polygon angle sums and use angle relationships to find missing values.
lessons.before: Draw all possible diagonals from one vertex in a convex polygon.
lessons.ideas:
A polygon with n sides splits into n minus 2 triangles. Each triangle adds 180°.

The exterior turns add to 360°. For a regular polygon, the turns are all the same.

Use corresponding or alternate angles in parallel lines, vertically opposite angles at a crossing, and triangle or quadrilateral sums as needed.
lessons.method:
Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.
mistakes: Do not count a side of the polygon as a diagonal.
An adjacent interior and exterior angle make 180°, not 360°.
Corresponding angles need parallel lines. A diagram that only looks parallel does not establish it.

examples.title: Find an interior angle sum
examples.question:
A community tile design is based on a convex polygon with 8 sides.

  1. Find the sum of its interior angles in degrees.

    [2]

  2. Does the sum require a regular polygon? Explain.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Draw diagonals from one vertex. The number of triangles is 6.

Each triangle contributes 180°, making 1080°.

\(1080\)

(b) A fan of diagonals still gives the same total for any convex polygon of this size.

No. The number of triangles depends on the sides, not their lengths.

examples.title: Walk once around a regular polygon
examples.question:
A robot walks the sides of a regular 90-sided polygon. It turns through the same angle at each vertex.

  1. Give the angle of each exterior turn in degrees.

    [2]

  2. Find a single interior angle.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) A complete circuit needs 360°. Share it equally among 90 turns.

\(4\)

(b) An exterior and its adjacent interior angle lie on a straight line.

176°.

examples.title: Trace an angle between parallels
examples.question:
A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One acute angle is 44°. A triangle uses a matching corresponding angle and another interior angle of 56°.

  1. Find the third angle in degrees.

    [2]

  2. State the relationship used for the first angle.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) The first interior angle equals 44° because corresponding angles in parallel lines are equal.

Subtract 44° and 56° from 180°.

\(80\)

(b) Both angles are in matching positions relative to a parallel line and the transversal.

Corresponding angles are equal.

lessons.title: Bearings, scales and constructions
lessons.summary: Read positions on maps and construct exact angles and regular polygons.
lessons.objective: Read positions on maps and construct exact angles and regular polygons.
lessons.before: Draw a north line through the point you start from.
lessons.ideas:
A bearing is stated with three digits. Reverse a bearing by adding or subtracting 180°.

Use a unit rate such as metres per centimetre. Multiply it by the measured map length.

Bisect 60° to get 30° or 90° to get 45°. Use equal compass arcs to find the line through the middle of each angle.

Share 360° equally at the centre to locate the vertices. A regular hexagon can also be stepped round with the radius as compass width.
lessons.method:
Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.

Show the step that explains your answer.
mistakes: North lines stay parallel at both locations on a plan.
Convert to the requested unit when giving the answer.
Keep the construction marks so a reader can see how you found the angle.
Use the angle at the centre, not the angle inside the polygon.

examples.title: Reverse a bearing
examples.question:
On a plan, the bearing of Q from P is 063°.

  1. Find the bearing of P from Q in degrees.

    [2]

  2. Give a reminder for writing a bearing.

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Draw a north line at Q parallel to the one at P. The opposite direction is half a full turn away.

Add 180° to 063°.

\(243\)

(b) A leading zero marks the position of the hundreds digit.

Use three digits measured clockwise from north.

examples.title: Use a plan scale
examples.question:
On a plan, 1 cm represents 170 m. A walking route measures 3 cm along a straight segment.

  1. Find the actual length in metres.

    [2]

  2. If the map were drawn at half its size, what happens to route length on the map?

    [1]
examples.solution:
(a) Use 170 m for each of 3 cm.

\(510\)

(b) The actual route length stays the same.

It is halved.

examples.title: Construct an exact angle
examples.question:
Draw a right angle on a 16 cm base. Use equal arcs inside the angle and join their crossing back to the vertex.

  1. Find the size of the constructed angle in degrees.

    [2]

  2. Construct the 45° angle on paper. Leave the compass arcs visible.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) The angle bisector splits 90° into two equal angles.

\(45\)

(b) Start with the stated base. Use a consistent compass width for each pair of arcs.

A 45° angle with usable construction marks.

examples.title: Construct a regular polygon
examples.question:
You want to draw a regular 6-sided polygon around a circle with radius 13 cm.

  1. Give the angle at the centre between successive vertices in degrees.

    [2]

  2. Describe how to finish the drawing from one marked vertex.

    [2]
examples.solution:
(a) Equal central angles divide the full 360° into 6 pieces.

\(60\)

(b) For a regular hexagon, the compass radius also equals its side length.

Mark the central angles consecutively and join neighbouring points on the circle.
